The old lighthouse keeper, Silas, had seen more storms than most men. Sixty years he’d tended the lamp, a solitary sentinel against the relentless churn of the sea. He knew the moods of the water, the language of the wind, the precise moment a squall would descend. But tonight, the sea was calm, a vast, obsidian mirror reflecting an impossible clarity. He felt a disquiet, a tremor under his skin that had nothing to do with the weather.

He’d always been a man of routines, of predictable rhythms. Yet, tonight, he found himself drawn to the seaward-facing window. The darkness wasn't simply the absence of light; it was a weight, a tangible pressure. It seemed to hum with a silent energy, pulling him towards it. He’d spent so many years observing the distant horizon, familiar with every rock, every shoal, every shifting sandbar. Now, that distance felt different, deeper somehow.

The mainland's lights were muted tonight, swallowed by the expanse. Beyond them, the world stretched onward, a black canvas sprinkled with a million points of light. But it wasn’t the stars that held his gaze. It was what lay *between*. An emptiness that defied comprehension. He’d gazed at those lights since he was a boy, imagining journeys to far-off lands, fantastical, probably ridiculous dreams. Tonight, the yearning felt… different.

He felt a peculiar kinship with the deep, vast darkness. A sense of longing, not for something he could name, but for something lost, something remembered. His thoughts drifted to stories his grandmother told him as a child, of shimmering pathways in the night sky, of worlds beyond imagining. He’ telescope was silent.

The silence amplified the stillness, almost oppressive. He traced a finger across the condensation on the windowpane, feeling a faint echo of the loneliness he’d carried for so long. It wasn’t the solitude of isolation, but the vastness of existence itself. His hand trembled slightly. It was a loneliness that encompassed everything.

The current lighthouse keeper's daughter, Elsie, was due to visit tomorrow. He tried to focus on that - the thrill of her laughter, her stories of the world beyond the island. He'd tell her countless tales of the sea, of the ships that had passed, the storms he had weathered.

But the immensity beckoned. He was aware of the tiny sphere of the lighthouse, his little patch of rock nestled in the churning world. He considered the immensity of space, the incomprehensible distances that separate us. He could feel an infinite expanse within himself.

He shifted his gaze back to the obsidian canvas, and for a long moment, he simply watched. He felt a profound sense of peace, for a moment, like he had already witnessed what he needed to see. Not with his eyes, but with something more… something deeper.
